Back with another very commonly asked question, something we see every day in my practice: how to treat rosacea.

#rosacea #dermatologist #skincare #facecare
transcript: Rosacea is a condition where we see redness on the face, usually central facial redness, so around the nose, forehead, chin, and it can be accompanied with acne bumps as well. And there are considered to be four types of rosacea. There's the erythematotelangiectatic type, which is just straight up redness, and then there's the papulopustular rosacea, so the rosacea that gets a lot of acne bumps associated with it. There's ocular rosacea, so you can get rosacea in your eyes, and then there's something called rhinophyma, where people get like a buildup of sebaceous tissue in their nose. like pretty big noses. When it comes to just basic skin care with rosacea, the main thing is just keeping things gentle. Gentle cleansers, gentle moisturizers, gentle sunscreens. I recommend mineral-based sunscreens over chemical sunscreens. Brands that I really like that have gentle cleansing ingredients are CeraVe, La Roche-Posay, Avène, and Aveeno, as well as their moisturizers.

transcript: Can you actually eat your skincare? Well, kind of. Now, there's no evidence whatsoever that eating carrots will deliver any meaningful amount of retinoid activity to your skin the way, like topical tretinoin or retinol does. But we actually have some decent human studies to show that certain foods and supplements can actually affect the way our skin ages. So, for example, tomatoes, which have lycopene, can actually increase your skin's resistance to UV damage. There's also cocoa, flavanols and other polyphenols that may help with things like elasticity and, like, photo Protection. And then oral collagen peptides do have some decent amount of data. I mean, a lot of its industry back, but they do have studies showing modest improvement in wrinkles, hydration, and elasticity after about three months of use. And then there's also some interesting data with things like green tea, astaxanthin and Omega threes. And we have some emerging data coming out with things like curcumin and resveratrol. But, and this is very important, none of these foods are gonna replace your tried and true skincare. Products like sunscreen, retinoids, and antioxidant serums like vitamin C have decades of research to show its impact on skin health and wrinkles and photo damage. Obviously, nutrition is really important to support your skin from the inside out. But I would not rely on diet alone to make your skin better.

current.subject: can you eat your skincare
current.claim: Foods like tomatoes and oral collagen modestly help skin aging, but they don't replace sunscreen, retinoids and vitamin C.

We're basically putting back the collagen that's depleted. Another very effective treatment is the use of emface. Emface is a basically a combination of muscle stimulation and radio frequency. By strengthening those muscles, it actually holds up the skin better, the lines diminish, and the radio frequency stimulates collagen.

title: Exosomes Skincare: Miracle or Overhyped?
caption:
Are exosomes the next big thing in skincare, or just an expensive fad? 
WATCH FULL VIDEO! -    • 12 Science-Backed Anti-Aging Skincare Ingr...  
Top facial plastic surgeon Dr. Amir Karam gives exosomes a generous yet still low rating, calling them one of the most overhyped ingredients on the market. Dr. Karam explains why there's currently no reliable evidence that these ingredients can penetrate the skin or deliver any proven regenerative benefits. Always be highly skeptical of products rushed
transcript: So Exazoos is up number 11. So Exazoos is probably in my mind one of the most overhyped skincare ingredients. First of all, let's start with what exoomes are. So they're basically think of them as packages. So think of them as like little bags that are technically supposed to keep in the bags some important cellular messengers. And the idea is that the this bag will then be able to penetrate through the cell surface, enter the cell, deliver those cellular messengers, things like growth factors and proteins that are, you know, would potentially regenerate and repair skin. The problem is at the moment I'm going to give Exoomes a 1 out of 10. And that's obviously being generous. And the reason why is because there's literally no evidence whatsoever that exoomes can penetrate the skin in a reliable way at this time. You know, like I said, there's smart research being done. There's labs out there trying to sort this out. But sometimes you come to market too quickly with something. All you have is some pre-clinical data, meaning like things that are done in in laboratories and cells and, you know, not on actual human skin and not specifically not done over time and not done in larger studies, etc. The way all the other ingredients that I just talked about have been done. You have to question this um because there's no standardization. And there's no proof of efficacy. And um even just the concentrations, how much of this is penetrating, how much is not, what is really happening at the cellular level. These things all lead me to be concerned about not just efficacy, but even safety, right? Right? We just simply don't have enough long-term data about their potential, but also their safety.
